entries.clue: Refs abused after boy band’s sporting feats (4-4)

indicatorNotes.abused: Letters that have been abused have been knocked about, so they come out in an order other than the one they were handed over in.
indicatorNotes.after: After sends the word in front of it to the back, so the knocked-about letters follow the band rather than opening the entry.

blocks.note: Five were the British boy band of the late nineties who put their name on records as 5ive
four letters rearranged

annotation.surface: Match officials taking abuse in the wake of a boy band's athletic triumphs.
annotation.walkthrough: A five-fer is cricket's shorthand for a bowler taking five wickets in an innings, spelt the way commentators say it. The hyphen in the enumeration is the clue's one honest signal that a number starts the entry.
annotation.definitionFit: Five-fers are hauls of five wickets in an innings, which is the kind of performance a scorecard records as a feat.

entries.clue: See 15
A couple short of a dozen legs – and joints? (6)

blocks.clueFragment: A couple short of a dozen
blocks.note: a dozen is twelve and a couple is two, so the arithmetic is done in words
in cricket the leg side of the wicket is also called the on side, so a leg is an on

annotation.surface: Counting up a creature that has two fewer than twelve legs, and wondering about its joints.
annotation.walkthrough: A tenon is the tongue of wood cut to fit a mortise, so the joints are carpentry rather than anatomy. Cricket's on side is the side the batter's legs stand on, which lets one word stand in for the other.
annotation.definitionFit: Tenons are the projecting tongues cut on a timber's end to slot into mortises, the joint that holds a frame or a chair together.

entries.clue: Burns fumes about cigar’s end (7)

indicatorNotes.about: Something placed about a thing is wrapped round it, so the letter named next goes into the middle.
indicatorNotes.end: The end of a word is where its final letter sits, so only that one letter is taken.

blocks.note: a kettle or a hot road fumes in the sense of giving off vapour
the last letter of cigar

annotation.surface: A man called Burns in a temper because his cigar has gone down to the stub.
annotation.walkthrough: A burn is a Scottish brook, which is why the capital B at the head of the clue can pretend to be a surname. 'Fumes' works twice over: rage on the surface, vapour underneath.
annotation.definitionFit: Burns are the small watercourses of Scotland and northern England, so the plural noun and the answer name the same running water.

entries.clue: See 22
Special few a part of ménages à trois? (10)

blocks.note: count the phrases standing in a row in front of the definition: there are three of them
and every one of the three says the same word — some as in 'that's some car', some as in a few, some as in a portion

annotation.surface: A particular handful of people making up part of a French three-cornered arrangement.
annotation.walkthrough: The wordplay counts words instead of letters, which is why nothing in it looks like fodder. 'Special' is the some of 'that's some car', and once all three openers are seen to be saying one word, their number supplies the rest.
annotation.definitionFit: A ménage à trois is a household of three people sharing a relationship, which is one sense of a threesome, and the French plural matches the plural answer.

entries.clue: Scratching surface of dark side in barrel (6)

indicatorNotes.in: What is in something sits inside it, so these letters are dropped into the middle of the word named next.

blocks.note: a keg is the small barrel beer is drawn from
in Chinese thought yin is the dark, shadowed half of the pair whose other half is yang

annotation.surface: Only beginning to look into the sinister business kept in a barrel.
annotation.walkthrough: To key a car is to drag a key along its paintwork, which is scratching a surface in the most deliberate way there is. 'Dark side' belongs to yin and yang, not to a villain.
annotation.definitionFit: Keying means dragging something sharp along paintwork, so the answer is the act of scratching a surface rather than a synonym for damage.

entries.clue: Painstaking papers back essentially glib man (8)

indicatorNotes.back: Back means the two letters are read the other way about, right to left along the row.
indicatorNotes.essentially: What is essential to a word lies at its heart, so the letters taken are the central ones.

blocks.note: ID is the identification a bouncer asks for, turned round
the two letters at the centre of the four
a gent is a man, as on the lavatory door

annotation.surface: A newspaper throwing its weight behind a smooth-talking man.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Papers' is the card in a wallet rather than the ones on the doormat, and turning it round is what gets the entry started. 'Essentially' asks for the heart of a word, never its gist.
annotation.definitionFit: Somebody diligent takes pains over a job, working at it steadily and thoroughly, which is what painstaking describes.

entries.clue: Badenoch reveals strain – of iron? (5)

indicatorNotes.reveals: To reveal something is to show what was there all along, so the letters are already written out in the clue in the right order.

blocks.note: Kemi Badenoch leads the Conservative party, and the run wanted does not stop where her name does

annotation.surface: The Conservative leader showing the streak of iron the press likes to compare with Thatcher's.
annotation.walkthrough: The surname is here for its letters rather than its politics, and the verb next to it is doing two jobs at once. 'Strain' means a variety, not tension, and this pigment's colour is rust — iron oxide.
annotation.definitionFit: Ochre is the iron-rich clay dug up and ground for pigment, so calling it a strain of iron names the earth by the metal that colours it.

entries.clue: Stable houses setter – was one lost? (4)

indicatorNotes.lost: What is lost is no longer among the letters, so the piece named beside it drops out of the word it was in.

blocks.note: the setter is the person writing the puzzle, who refers to himself as me
three letters, taken as they stand
a is the article that means one, as in a dozen for one dozen

annotation.surface: A stable with a setter living in it, and the question of whether one has gone missing.
annotation.walkthrough: The setter is the compiler signing himself in, not the gun dog the stable invites you to picture. Losing 'one' means losing an A, which is the commonest way a clue asks for that letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A mews is a row of old stables converted into dwellings, so the plural noun names stables and houses in one breath.

entries.clue: Regarding those unidentified, technology goes too far (8,2)

blocks.note: a row over money is a row regarding money, so over can mean concerning
an unidentified person in an American court is a John or a Jane Doe, so several of them are Does
IT is information technology, the department that mends the laptops

annotation.surface: A memo about unidentified persons, complaining that the technology has got out of hand.
annotation.walkthrough: John Doe and Jane Doe are the American names for people whose identity is unknown, so more than one of them is a plural. 'Over' here is the preposition meaning concerning, the sense in 'an argument over money'.
annotation.definitionFit: To overdo it is to push something past the sensible point, which is what going too far describes.

entries.clue: Savages live, pasts quietly forgotten (6)

indicatorNotes.forgotten: What has been forgotten is no longer there, so the letter named beside it goes missing from the word before.

blocks.note: to be is to live, as in let me be
five letters, the word the deletion works on
p is piano on a score, the instruction to play softly

annotation.surface: Savage men still alive, their histories conveniently forgotten.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Savages' looks like the verb a critic does to a book and is in fact the noun, the wild things themselves. Piano is the softest marking a composer writes, which is why quiet is p in hundreds of clues.
annotation.definitionFit: Beasts are wild animals and, said of people, brutes, which is exactly the plural noun savages names.

entries.clue: Here solstice worshipping teens go wild, gobbling bird (10)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is locative rather than a noun: the answer names the place where solstice worship happens, with 'here' pointing at it and the rest saying which place is meant.

indicatorNotes.go wild: Letters told to go wild stop behaving, and they will not come back in the order they were given.
indicatorNotes.gobbling: To gobble a thing is to swallow it whole, so what is named next is taken inside.

blocks.note: seven letters shuffled, and they part in the middle to take the bird
a hen is the female of the farmyard bird

annotation.surface: Teenagers who worship the solstice running riot at a spot, wolfing down poultry.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface paints the midsummer crowd at a stone circle and the answer is that circle, so picture and place turn out to be one. 'Gobbling' has to be swallowing here, never the noise a turkey makes.
annotation.definitionFit: Stonehenge is the Wiltshire circle where crowds gather to watch the sun come up at midsummer, so 'here' is pointing straight at it.

entries.clue: Video game reversed practice: that’s not right (8)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a verdict rather than a noun phrase: it passes judgement on the practice instead of naming it, which is how a comment comes to stand for the thing commented on.

indicatorNotes.reversed: Reversed means read the other way about, so the three letters in front of it turn round.

blocks.note: a sim, short for simulation, is the video game that models flying or farming, and it is turned round
usage is established practice, the way a thing is customarily done

annotation.surface: Someone playing a video game backwards and grumbling that the practice is wrong.
annotation.walkthrough: The trap is 'practice: that's not right', which reads as one grumble and is two jobs — the last piece of wordplay, then the definition. Sims are the simulation games, the flight and life kind.
annotation.definitionFit: Misusage is language used wrongly, the wrong word in the wrong place, so naming it by the verdict it earns is fair enough.

entries.clue: Golden age – at end of festivities? (7)

indicatorNotes.at end of: What sits at the end of a word is its closing letters, so only the tail of the word that follows is taken.

blocks.note: the tail of the word opens with VI, which is the Roman way of writing six, and the numeral is written out in English
the four letters that finish the word

annotation.surface: The best part of a celebration, arriving as the festivities come to an end.
annotation.walkthrough: All of the wordplay is in the tail of a single word, read first as a Roman numeral and then as plain English. The Sixties are called a golden age of music, and the decade of a life gets called the golden years too.
annotation.definitionFit: The Sixties is the decade regularly called a golden age of music and change, and a person's sixties are the golden years of a life.

entries.clue: Drugs cost (including recipe) negotiable for gigolos (7)

indicatorNotes.including: Including throws the letter named next in among the others, so it joins the pool waiting to be shuffled.
indicatorNotes.negotiable: A price that is negotiable can be moved about, and so can the letters the word is standing beside.

blocks.note: e is ecstasy, so more than one tablet is Es
four letters waiting to be rearranged
r stands for recipe, the Latin instruction written at the head of a prescription

annotation.surface: A street price for drugs with the recipe thrown in, open to haggling by men who sell company.
annotation.walkthrough: Escort is the trade's polite word for someone paid for their company, and the definition only makes it male. The bracket is not decoration: it says the odd letter joins the others before any shuffling happens.
annotation.definitionFit: Gigolos are men paid to squire women about, which is what male escorts advertise themselves as doing.

entries.clue: These world leaders on Russian river? It’s … it’s worth little in America (3,4)

annotation.definitionNote: Two bits is a noun, an American quarter, while the definition talks about worth: it is pointing at the idiom in which anything two-bit is dismissed as trifling.

indicatorNotes.leaders: The leaders of words are the letters at their head, so one letter is taken from the front of each.

blocks.note: the opening letter of each of the two words
the Ob is one of the great Siberian rivers, flowing north into the Arctic
the apostrophe is dropped, as crossword spelling always allows

annotation.surface: World leaders meeting on a Russian river, and a shrug about how little the whole thing is worth.
annotation.walkthrough: Two bits is twenty-five cents — a bit was an eighth of a Spanish dollar — so the phrase is American for small change. The row of dots is the surface trailing off and hides nothing.
annotation.definitionFit: Two bits is American slang for a quarter, and anything called two-bit over there is being dismissed as cheap.

entries.clue: Excuses politician embraced by alien in sex romp (7)

indicatorNotes.embraced by: To be embraced is to be held with arms either side, so these letters go inside the ones named next.
indicatorNotes.in: In puts what has been assembled so far inside the letters that follow.
indicatorNotes.romp: A romp is a boisterous tumble, and letters that have been tumbled do not land in their old order.

blocks.note: three letters shuffled into a wrapper that opens after the first two
ET has been the crossword extraterrestrial since the film
an MP is a Member of Parliament

annotation.surface: A politician caught in an alien's arms during a sex romp.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Excuses' is the verb — what a tax rule does for you — rather than the noun a schoolboy offers. The wrapping happens twice, the smaller parcel going inside the bigger one before anything else is read.
annotation.definitionFit: To exempt somebody is to let them off a duty everyone else has to meet, which is what excusing them from it amounts to.

entries.clue: Settlers erected timber frames (8)

indicatorNotes.erected: Erected means put up out of parts, and a thing built from the same parts stands in a different arrangement.

blocks.note: eight letters waiting to be built up again

annotation.surface: Pioneers putting up wooden structures at their new settlement.
annotation.walkthrough: Trestles are the splayed wooden legs a plank rests on — a pasting table stands on a pair. The difficulty is that fodder and definition sit flush against each other with only the instruction between them.
annotation.definitionFit: A trestle is a braced wooden frame, and two of them under a board make a table, so timber frames names them plainly.

entries.clue: Confused? Yes – call in dope dispenser (7)

indicatorNotes.Confused: Letters described as confused have been muddled and no longer stand in the order the clue gave them.
indicatorNotes.in: In drops the piece just named inside the letters already assembled.

blocks.note: three letters muddled, and they come apart to make room
to ring somebody is to call them

annotation.surface: A bewildered admission, and a phone call to whoever hands the dope out.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dope' is the drug here, not the fool, and the thing that dispenses it goes into a vein. The question mark after the first word is the setter asking whether you are, which is also the instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: A syringe is what a drug is pushed through into the bloodstream, so it dispenses dope in the most literal way there is.

entries.clue: Otherwise show one mercy in service (8)

indicatorNotes.Otherwise: Otherwise means in some other way, and letters taken another way are letters taken in another order.

blocks.note: three letters of the fodder
and the five that complete it

annotation.surface: A plea for somebody to be shown mercy in the middle of a church service.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Show one mercy' is a whole idiom on the surface and no more than a bag of letters underneath. A service is a ceremony whether it is a wedding, a funeral or a christening.
annotation.definitionFit: A service — wedding, funeral, memorial — is a formal ceremony, so the two nouns name the same occasion.

entries.clue: England collapse over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over (10)

annotation.definition: over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over

blocks.note: a cricket team is eleven players, which is why a national side is called an eleven
a business or a poker hand that collapses folds

annotation.surface: England's batting caving in over after over after over.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is not described but performed: count the repetitions and the number is the one the entry opens with. An over is six balls of cricket, which is what makes the collapse funny.
annotation.definitionFit: Anything done over and over eleven times has happened elevenfold, so the printed repetition acts the definition out instead of stating it.

entries.clue: Revelling used to put out (6)

indicatorNotes.Revelling: To revel is to carouse without restraint, and letters doing that will not keep to their places.

blocks.note: four letters of the fodder
and the two that finish it

annotation.surface: Partying that once had a habit of annoying the neighbours.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Put out' carries three senses worth trying — annoyed, extinguished and thrown out — and the entry wants the third. The fodder is the everyday phrase standing in front of it, which reads as tense rather than letters.
annotation.definitionFit: To oust somebody is to drive them from a post or a property, so a leader who has been ousted has been put out of office.

entries.clue: ‘Aussie’ (not American) nightwear (6)

indicatorNotes.not: Not put in front of a thing is the instruction to take that thing out of the letters you already have.

blocks.note: the quotation marks mark the nickname as six letters to be cut about rather than a person
US is the everyday short form of the United States, and those are the two letters to go
the surgery leaves a lone A at the front, and A is a way of writing one, as in a dozen for one dozen

annotation.surface: An Australian's sleeping outfit, as distinct from an American's.
annotation.walkthrough: The quotation marks are the signal that the word itself is the raw material, not the man wearing it. A onesie is the all-in-one lounging suit British adults took up around 2012, borrowed from the babygro.
annotation.definitionFit: A onesie is the one-piece suit, babies' or adults', that people sleep and slouch about in, which is what nightwear covers.

entries.clue: Football seen around half ten, with commentary for audience (5-1-4)

indicatorNotes.around: What goes around a thing is wrapped about it, so the letter named next lands in the middle.
indicatorNotes.half: Half is one of two equal parts, and the number beside it is the Roman numeral, a character that splits cleanly down the middle.

blocks.note: four letters that open in the middle
ten in Roman numerals is X, and the top or bottom half of that character is V, the Roman five
an aside is the remark an actor turns and delivers to the audience over the other characters' heads

annotation.surface: A football match caught at about half past ten, with commentary laid on for the crowd.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Half ten' is a time of day on the surface and half a Roman numeral underneath, which is the whole of the clue's trick. Seven-a-side is the short-pitch game, played with four fewer than a full team.
annotation.definitionFit: Seven-a-side is football played with seven to a team instead of eleven, so the answer names a form of the game itself.

entries.clue: Affected Reform UK, say, with head removed (4)

indicatorNotes.say: Say marks what comes before it as an example, so the word wanted is the general class the named thing belongs to.
indicatorNotes.removed: Removed means taken away, so the letter named beside it does not appear in the answer.

blocks.note: Reform UK is one of Britain's political parties, the one Nigel Farage leads
the head of a word is its first letter

annotation.surface: Reform UK putting on airs now that its leader has been got rid of.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Say' is the flag that Reform UK is only an instance of the word wanted, a device worth spotting early because it never contributes letters of its own. Arty means affected about art, the pose rather than the ability.
annotation.definitionFit: Somebody arty makes a show of artistic taste, which is affectation rather than art, and affected is the word for that pose.

entries.clue: See 17 Down
See 27 Across
Pool party after nude hen night not new (5-4)

indicatorNotes.after: After sends the word in front of it to the back, so the party finishes the entry rather than starting it.
indicatorNotes.nude: Nude is with the clothes off, so the word loses the letters on its outside and only its middle is left.
indicatorNotes.not: Not takes away what it names, so that letter is missing from the word standing before it.

blocks.note: the middle letter, once the outer two are stripped away
five letters, the word the deletion works on
n is the standard abbreviation for new
a ball is a formal dance, the grandest sort of party

annotation.surface: A pool party following a hen night that nobody bothered to get dressed for.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pool party' looks like one phrase and is two jobs — the definition, then a word that only has to mean ball. Eight-ball is the pub game in which the black goes down last, and the black itself.
annotation.definitionFit: Eight-ball is the form of pool played on pub tables everywhere, named for the black ball that has to be sunk at the end.

entries.clue: More graceful win; limper member abandoned (8)

indicatorNotes.abandoned: What has been abandoned has been left behind, so the letters named are dropped from the word in front.

blocks.note: to gain is to win — ground, time, an advantage
six letters, the word the deletion works on
a Member of Parliament is an MP, and members is what the Commons calls them

annotation.surface: A victory looking better once the hobbling member has dropped out of the race.
annotation.walkthrough: Gainly is the word 'ungainly' was built from, still in the dictionary and almost never said aloud, which is why the comparative looks so odd. The semicolon is punctuation, not instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: Gainly means shapely or graceful, the positive that survives mainly inside its own negative, so gainlier is more graceful.
